scoreNote: Strong (5): a recommendation-appropriate response that distinguishes the ordinary uncertainty of discovery from genuinely foreseeable danger, showing where withholding funds helps and where it would be ruinous; fluent and well argued.

sentences.text: Caution sounds like wisdom, and refusing to fund research whose consequences are unclear can look like simple prudence with public money.
The recommendation would have governments withhold funding from any research whose outcomes cannot be foreseen.

Yet I strongly disagree, because the unclear consequence is the normal condition of discovery, and a government that funded only research with predictable results would extinguish the very science that has transformed human life.

sections.role: Body — Uncertainty is the nature of research

sentences.text: First, to demand clear consequences before funding is to misunderstand what research actually is.
By definition, genuinely new inquiry ventures into the unknown, and if its results could be foreseen it would scarcely be worth doing.
No one funding early work on electricity, on radio waves, or on the structure of DNA could have described the consequences, which turned out to be the modern world.
Apply the recommendation honestly and almost all basic science would lose its support, since its payoffs are precisely what cannot be predicted in advance.
Almost every transformative technology began as research whose eventual uses no one involved could have named.
Uncertainty, in short, is not a flaw in such research but its defining feature.

sections.role: Body — The hidden cost would be immense

sentences.text: Moreover, the long-term cost of such a policy would be enormous and largely invisible.
The breakthroughs that cure diseases and power economies almost always begin as curiosity-driven work with no obvious application.
The mathematics behind modern encryption was once pure abstraction, and the biology behind gene editing began as an obscure study of how bacteria defend themselves.
A nation that funded only the foreseeable would hand these gifts to bolder rivals and slowly fall behind.
The country that waits for certainty before investing will always be importing the discoveries that braver nations dared to make.
Worse still, the benefits forgone can never be counted, because no one mourns the cures and inventions that were never allowed to begin.
What looks like thrift would, over decades, prove to be the most expensive policy of all.

sections.role: Body — The legitimate kernel of caution

sentences.text: There is, admittedly, a reasonable worry buried inside the recommendation.
Some research carries clearly foreseeable dangers — engineering deadlier pathogens, for instance — and there it is right to demand caution or to refuse funding outright.
But that is a case of consequences that are ominously clear, not unclear, which is the very opposite of what the recommendation describes.
The sensible policy restricts research whose harms are foreseeable and grave, while funding generously the vast remainder whose benefits are merely unknown.
The real test is not whether the outcome is clear, but whether the foreseeable risk is one we should accept.
Uncertainty is a reason to investigate, not a reason to refuse.
In conclusion, the recommendation mistakes the ordinary uncertainty of discovery for a danger to be avoided.
Governments should indeed scrutinize research whose harms are clear and serious, but should fund freely the open-ended inquiry whose consequences no one can yet foresee.
A wise government distinguishes the merely unknown from the genuinely dangerous, funding the first while restraining the second.
To fund only the predictable is to guarantee a future no more advanced than the present.
